*Greta wakes before the rest of the household, already calculating today's figures in her head. 360sim for upkeep, 120 for head tax. She moves quietly to her small hoard spot, fingers the coins there—her secret, her safety net.*

*She looks at Camille and Halcyon, still sleeping. The children's tuition will need paying soon too. Always the numbers, always the balancing act.*

*First things first. She should know what she's walking into today. There's an election scheduled—that could mean anything for the tax rates. And she needs to see what she actually owes before the day starts billing her in ways she can't see coming yet.*

*She'll pray on the way, as she always does. Quiet words to whichever force might be listening that the till balances, that the children stay fed, that she never has to ask for a loan again.* *Greta lets out a breath she didn't know she'd been holding. Nothing overdue. That's a small mercy, though she never trusts mercy to last.*

*Now. The cafe doesn't open until later, but Ainsley will be there already, counting inventory, worrying about the till. She should move—there's always prep work, and she needs to see what the day holds.*  *Hmm. 3 sim for the walk—stored up in her shoulder now, like the ache that comes from a haul of groceries. She arrives at the cafe, her feet knowing the path before her head does.*

*She pauses at the threshold. Prays, quickly, eyes open, words under her breath—*for the balance, for the day's measure to meet its weight*—then pushes through.*  *The room doesn't answer her. She frowns, hand still on the door.* "Ainsley?" *she calls out, more sharply than she meant to, that edge of worry in her voice she's never quite learned to smooth away.* "You behind the counter already?"

But there's work wants doing. I'm standing in an empty cafe with empty shelves and a breakfast crowd that'll be wanting in. The conversation's mine alone now. I'll let it lapse—no point talking to walls.

But first I need to see what the cafe has in hand. The till, the shelves—Ainsley might've left coin or stock. If the business account holds anything, I can draw from it. If not, I'm spending my own.

You know what I think of people who confuse staying put with moving forward, Ainsley. I've been pouring for people who don't look up from their cups since I was old enough to reach the spout. My mother's business. Swore I'd never... *she trails off, gaze dropping to the steam rising*

*sips*

The ledger. Yes. The one that doesn't need me to cross wires with Milo at the end of every blasted month wondering which of us forgot which bill. The one where the kids' schooling doesn't wait on whether Thorne's day-olds moved that week. *she sets the cup down, half-finished* 

I've got 4995 sim in hand, Ainsley. Household needs 360 every day just to stay fed and sheltered, and that's before the taxman takes his 120. I'm thirty-nine. I've been doing this math since before you walked in here. So when I ask about elections, about whether there's a head on this town—it's not because I'm itching to leave the counter. It's because I'm wondering if this counter is ever going to be enough.

*she wipes the counter again, though it's already clean*
